articles.title: An acetylcholine-inhibited sleep-active hippocampal interneuron orchestrates memory consolidation.
articles.authors: Feng Y, Dai Q, Fei X, Yang H, Jiang T, Liu Z, Ye L, Lin Z, Gao S, Hu R, Li X, Liu R, Peng W, Xu M.
articles.abstract: Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). Suppressing their activity in dorsal CA3 or ventral hippocampus impaired spatial and social memory, respectively. Furthermore, Chrm2+ neurons were closely associated with ripples; their activity bidirectionally modulated ripple occurrence via widespread inhibition. Thus, Chrm2+ interneurons are critical in linking neuromodulatory state to memory consolidation, offering genetically targeted access to sleep-active memory circuits implicated in cognitive disorders.

articles.title: Purely Mechanical Muscle Length Feedback Enables Embodied Reflexive Control in Musculoskeletal Robots
articles.authors: Shunsuke Koseki, Mitsuhiro Hayashibe, Dai Owaki
articles.abstract: Reflexes are a fundamental principle of biological movement; however, their application in musculoskeletal robots has been limited due to reliance on complex electronic sensing and control systems. This study presents the first implementation of the muscle length feedback reflex and establishes a minimal sensorimotor unit based on mechanical intelligence. Specifically, the proposed reflex module integrates sensing, computation, and actuation within its physical architecture, enabling autonomous contraction when muscle length exceeds a threshold, entirely without electronic components. Additionally, a muscle spindle‐inspired mechanism allows for adaptive modulation of this threshold. When incorporated into musculoskeletal robots, the module reproduced the patellar tendon reflex. Furthermore, by integrating this mechanical reflex with high‐level phase‐dependent threshold modulation control, bipedal locomotion was generated as an emergent behavior. These findings demonstrate that essential local sensorimotor control can be physically realized within mechanical systems, providing a minimal, robust, and scalable design principle for musculoskeletal robotics and advancing embodied intelligence beyond traditional control architectures.

articles.title: Generalizable neural decoding for clinically scalable brain-computer interfaces
articles.authors: Yuanjie Gu, Haotian Yin, Yiqun Wang
articles.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces promise restored communication and movement, yet accuracy achieved under development rarely survives new sessions, users, tasks, or hardware. Generalization, not peak performance, determines clinical scalability. Here we examine generalizable neural decoding from development to deployment, organized by the domain held out at evaluation, target-data access, adaptation strategy, and the clinical conditions under which performance persists, identifying benchmarking standards, prospective validation, and hardware-algorithm co-design as prerequisites for durable benefit.

articles.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models
articles.authors: Peisong Wen, Qianqian Xu, Minye Lei
articles.abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.

articles.title: EndoWorld-JEPA: Motion-Guided Global-Local Latent World Modeling for Endoscopic Video Representation Learning
articles.authors: Jie Wang, Shilong Yang, Tao Zhou
articles.abstract: Endoscopic video contains state transitions induced by camera displacement, deformable tissue, and instrument interaction, yet existing pre-training methods treat dynamics implicitly. Inspired by action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive world models and by the observation that endoscopic optical flow contains both shared image-plane displacement and localized residual motion, we reformulate passive endoscopic video pre-training as causal motion-guided latent-state prediction. We present EndoWorld-JEPA, to our knowledge the first latent world-model pre-training framework designed for general-purpose endoscopic video representation learning. In place of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics, the model conditions prediction of the next latent state on motion observed up to the current state. Its Optical Motion-guided module separates dominant displacement from residual motion and converts the resulting evidence into an ordered temporal motion condition and spatial local-motion weights. Complementary global and motion-local predictors use these outputs: the temporal condition modulates both latent transitions, whereas the local weights define an auxiliary motion-local state that extends prediction from scene-level evolution to spatially selective dynamics. Patch-wise motion weighting emphasizes localized change while retaining anatomical context, and past-motion-window dropout randomly withholds the complete motion condition to reduce dependence on unreliable motion. This global--local formulation learns predictable visual--motion dynamics in representation space without reconstructing stochastic appearance artifacts. Evaluation shows that a common pre-trained checkpoint achieves strong transfer across four downstream benchmarks, supporting motion-guided global--local latent prediction as an effective pre-training paradigm for endoscopic video.

articles.title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
articles.authors: Hossein Resani, Javen Qinfeng Shi
articles.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.

articles.title: Effect of robotic assistance on upper-limb sensorimotor recovery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Ritwika Choudhuri, John Michael Solomon, Aravind Nehrujee
articles.abstract: Introduction Robot-assisted upper-limb neurorehabilitation enables several beneficial therapy components, including repetitive task-specific practice, high training intensity, real-time feedback, gamification, and continuous physical interaction with the patient’s limb. However, conventional comparisons of robot-assisted and therapist-delivered rehabilitation cannot determine whether the physical assistance provided by the robot contributes independently to recovery. This systematic review and meta-analysis, therefore, focused specifically on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of upper-limb rehabilitation in which experimental and comparator interventions were designed to be similar except for the presence, or level, or mode of robotic assistance. Methods PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched through November 2025 for eligible studies. Study screening and filtration were performed using Covidence software. Thirteen studies met the eligibility criteria for qualitative synthesis, and nine studies involving 272 stroke survivors provided Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) data for quantitative synthesis. The standardized mean difference (SMD) between the control and the experimental group for change in pre-to-post intervention FMA score was calculated to perform meta-analysis. Heterogeneity computation, sensitivity analysis, risk of bias, publication bias, and certainty of evidence evaluation were also performed. Results The main meta-analysis pooled effect (SMD = 0.425) favored the experimental robot-assisted condition across disease stages, assistance levels, and targeted limb segments. However, this overall effect was imprecise (95% CI: [−0.007, 0.858]) and showed substantial heterogeneity (62.62%). In studies restricted to chronic stroke, the pooled effect was larger (SMD = 0.53), although imprecision [0.067, 0.992] and heterogeneity (60.72%) remained similar. Estimates for shoulder-elbow and hand-focused interventions were small and imprecise too. Sensitivity analyses showed that the direction of the pooled effect was stable across various considerations. The certainty of evidence was judged to be low, primarily because of risk of bias concerns (mainly lack of double-blinding), inconsistency, and imprecision. Exploratory meta-regression did not identify clear study-level moderators of between-study heterogeneity. In addition, no significant publication bias was identified. Discussion Although this study provides preliminary evidence suggesting a positive independent influence of the robotic assistance on upper-limb recovery, the limited number of studies with their small sample sizes and substantial heterogeneity preclude a firm conclusion. Larger, adequately powered RCTs that isolate robotic physical assistance while standardizing other intervention components are needed to establish its independent causal contribution to upper-limb sensorimotor recovery.

articles.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
articles.authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Sicheng Liu, Haiyu Wu
articles.abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.

articles.title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning via Algorithmic Stability
articles.authors: Guodong Zheng, Yan Sun, Peng Wang
articles.abstract: Understanding catastrophic forgetting, in which learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned tasks, remains a fundamental challenge in continual learning (CL). Existing theoretical analyses often rely on specific model or task structures and offer limited insight into how iterative optimization affects forgetting. To address this gap, we develop an algorithmic stability framework for expected population forgetting under SGD without prescribing a particular model architecture. Specifically, we decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting. To bound the generalization gaps, we track how a sample perturbation affects updates within a task and propagates through subsequent tasks. We consider constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules. Comparing the two decaying schedules allows us to characterize how restarting learning-rate decay at task boundaries affects the propagation of historical sample perturbations. For empirical forgetting, we derive bounds for all three schedules by retaining cumulative gradient alignment along the optimization trajectory, without requiring convexity. Combining these results yields upper bounds on expected forgetting that capture the effects of training set size, the number of updates per task, the total number of tasks, learning-rate schedules, and cumulative gradient alignment. Finally, we conduct experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet to examine the empirical implications of our theoretical findings.

articles.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
articles.authors: Yicheng Xu, Z. Xu, Ziyuan Chen
articles.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

articles.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
articles.authors: Yanzhe Chen, Ziyi Yang, Jifeng Zhu
articles.abstract: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

articles.title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
articles.authors: Feng Chen, Pei Zhou, Lixuan He
articles.abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/

articles.title: Towards semantic brain-computer interfacing: The graded inventory of semantic triggers (GIST) paradigm
articles.authors: Joshua James Podmore, Moein Radman, Riccardo Poli
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Semantic Brain-Computer Interfaces (sBCIs) aim to decode conceptual information directly from neural activity, enabling more efficient and natural communication for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, existing approaches are often confounded by stimulus-driven perceptual processes and lack a reliable means of tagging the moment of concept formation. We introduce the Graded Inventory of Semantic Triggers (GIST), a novel electroencephalography (EEG) paradigm designed to elicit semantic retrieval from graded verbal clues with precise temporal alignment. Approach: EEG data were recorded from 14 participants performing the GIST task across three semantic categories (food, musical instruments, and body parts). Target neural activity was aligned to each participant's self-reported moment of semantic retrieval (spacebar press), enabling response-locked analysis. Here, we propose a staged framework where the first comprises a Conformer-based encoder trained on pooled data using a hybrid contrastive objective that combines instance-level consistency and cross-participant class alignment with domain-adversarial learning to reduce participant-specific information. In the second stage, the frozen encoder is transferred to a held-out participant whose data played no part in Stage 1, and a support vector machine is calibrated on that participant's own labelled items under a nested leave-one-item-out protocol. Results: Above-chance semantic decoding was achieved in all three pairwise tasks. Mean accuracies were 73.4% (Body vs. Food), 70.7% (Body vs. Music), and 68.2% (Food vs. Music). Participant-level permutation tests were significant in 9/11 participants for Body vs. Food and 8/11 for each of the other tasks (p < 0.05). The pre-response interval at [-1.5s, -0.5s] was the most discriminative. Significance: The GIST paradigm enables controlled elicitation and temporal alignment of semantic processing while reducing perceptual confounds. Combined with cross-participant representation pretraining and participant-specific calibration, the results demonstrate above-chance decoding of semantic categories from EEG in individuals excluded from representation learning, supporting the feasibility of sBCIs.

articles.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
articles.authors: Motoshige Sato, Eri Hatakeyama, Masakazu Inoue
articles.abstract: Abstract Objective . Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance . Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.

articles.title: ForagerSim: Evaluating Embodied Map-Based Reasoning in Large-Scale Dynamic Worlds
articles.authors: Tomáš Musil, Martin Kotík, Michal Vavrečka
articles.abstract: Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces. In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all. Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning. To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks). We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods. Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.

articles.title: Temporal instability weakens entorhinal grid-like coding in older adults
articles.authors: Vladislava Segen, Gerard Callau Navarro, Philip Bahrd
articles.abstract: Entorhinal grid cell representations are thought to support spatial navigation and episodic memory, functions that decline with age. Their putative fMRI correlate, the hexadirectional signal, varies markedly among older adults, but the source of this variability is unknown. Using virtual navigation and fMRI in 85 older adults, we tested whether signal strength was related to the stability of hexadirectional signals. Hexadirectional orientation stability, the cross-run reproducibility of direction-specific activity patterns, was associated with hexadirectional signal strength in the posterior-medial-entorhinal-cortex (pmEC). In left-pmEC, higher orientation stability also predicted better object-location memory. In contrast, age and local structural measures did not account for individual differences in either measure. Finally, retrosplenial absolute-orientation stability was associated with left-pmEC orientation stability, and a mediation analysis supported an indirect association with hexadirectional signals through pmEC orientation stability. Together, these findings suggest that weaker entorhinal hexadirectional signal in aging may reflect unstable, rather than absent, entorhinal grid-cell-like representations.

articles.title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
articles.authors: Yilei Man, Yang Chen, Jingcai Guo
articles.abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.

articles.title: Trustworthy Imagination in Embodied World Models: Structural Constraints, Reality Anchoring, and Trust Adjudication
articles.authors: Chenwei Shi, Xueyu Luan, Shuo Jiang
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT World models provide embodied agents with a mechanism for planning, policy improvement, and adaptation through imagined futures before physical‐world execution. However, such imagination is useful only when it is trustworthy: predicted futures must respect action dependence, temporal order, task intent, embodiment, contact, and the limits of available real‐world evidence. This survey organizes recent world‐model research around a mechanism‐level question: which design mechanisms make imagined futures reliable enough to guide control? We identify three coupled governance roles that intervene at different points in the evidence chain. Structural constraint shapes which futures may be imagined through causal rollout and autoregressive memory, predictive abstraction, conditioned and controllable generation, and physical structure, signals, and constraints. Reality anchoring ties imagined futures to real evidence through data‐scaled and cross‐embodied priors, perceptual and geometric anchors, and reality‐grounded post‐training loops. Trust adjudication determines how imagined futures may be used through rollout constraints and scoring, runtime diagnostics and response, and offline evaluation and benchmarks. Overall, this mechanism‐first taxonomy clarifies why visual plausibility is not enough: reliable imagination depends on coordinating what the model is allowed to generate, how its predictions are anchored to evidence, and when those predictions are permitted to influence downstream decisions.

articles.title: Hierarchical Interoceptive–Social Inference Dysregulation: A Computational Psychiatry Framework for Borderline Personality Disorder with Level-1 Active Inference Simulation and Implications for Cluster B Pathology
articles.authors: Marco Fronzi
articles.abstract: Abstract Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), the prototypic Cluster B condition, is characterised by profound instability in affect, self-image, and interpersonal relationships, including rapid oscillation between idealisation and devaluation. Despite decades of neurobiological and psychotherapeutic research, no unified mechanistic theory accounts for the simultaneous presence of interoceptive dysregulation, interpersonal hypersensitivity, unstable identity, and splitting. Here we (i) review the hot research topics in Cluster B personality disorders in the recent literature, including triple-network neuroimaging dysconnectivity, allostatic interoceptive overload, and computational psychiatry approaches; (ii) identify the critical gap — the absence of a formal mechanistic account coupling interoceptive and social predictive hierarchies; (iii) propose the Hierarchical Interoceptive–Social Inference Dysregulation (HISID) framework, positing that BPD arises from a precision dissociation in which interoceptive precision is chronically suppressed while social-threat precision is pathologically elevated, leaving the self-model anchored exclusively to volatile social-affective inputs; and (iv) present a Level-1 computational simulation implementing two active inference agents — a healthy control (HC) and a BPD agent characterised by suppressed interoceptive precision, asymmetric social-threat amplification, a bimodal (splitting) social prior, and a hysteresis commitment mechanism — embedded in a 300-trial social-threat paradigm. While the HISID framework is introduced within the broader context of Cluster B personality disorders, the formal theory, parameterisation, simulations, and empirical predictions presented in this paper are specific to BPD as the prototypic Cluster B condition. Extension of the precision-dissociation formalism to narcissistic, antisocial, and histrionic personality disorders — each of which is predicted to occupy a distinct parametric region within the same generative architecture — is deferred to subsequent work. Across $$n=40$$ agents per group, the BPD agent produces a 4.22 $$\times $$ increase in self-model variance, a 10.33 $$\times $$ increase in per-agent median threat-recovery time, and a 4.45 $$\times $$ increase in unweighted cumulative prediction-error accumulation (alongside a 2.61 $$\times $$ increase in precision-weighted free energy; the unweighted measure is reported as a control on precision-induced mechanical scaling). A factorial control study crossing precision profile with generative architecture decomposes the BPD phenotype into distinct contributions: identity-instability variance is driven primarily by the bimodal-prior architecture, whereas threat-recovery slowing is driven primarily by the asymmetric threat-conditional precision, with a super-additive interaction in the full agent. These differences are large and internally consistent within the simulation and constitute demonstrations of model sufficiency, not empirical theory validation. A sensitivity analysis across a $$3\times 3$$ precision grid confirms qualitative robustness. A key architectural finding is that the bimodal prior requires Bayesian mixture belief updating with hysteresis commitment — not gradient descent — providing a candidate formalisation of splitting as discrete pole-occupancy inference. The HISID framework, grounded in the Free Energy Principle, generates five operationalised empirical predictions testable with existing neuroimaging and computational phenotyping methods.

articles.title: High-Resolution Spatial Proteomics Uncovers Molecular Diversity across Mouse Hippocampal Subregions
articles.authors: Zhangyang Xu, Jessie Shi, Reta Birhanu Kitata
articles.abstract: Abstract The hippocampus (HP) is a structurally and functionally heterogeneous brain region critical for learning, memory, and spatial navigation. Although transcriptomic studies have revealed subregion-specific gene expression patterns, the corresponding high-resolution spatial proteomic landscape remains largely unexplored. Here, we applied a single-voxel proteomics workflow at 50 μm resolution to profile the protein composition of HP subregions, including the dentate gyrus (DG) and Cornu Ammonis fields 1–3 (CA1–CA3). Across the four subregions, we identified over 2,200 protein groups and found both conserved and region-specific proteins. Differential expression and network analyses revealed molecular signatures associated with specific subregions, including synaptic plasticity in CA1, mitochondrial metabolism in CA2, cytoskeletal organization and protein homeostasis in CA3, and excitatory signaling in DG. Integration with transcriptomic data confirmed consistent region-enriched markers at both the gene and protein levels, including Homer1 and Itpka in CA1, Homer3 in CA3, and Calb1/2 in DG. Thus, our data set demonstrates subregion-specific molecular specialization at the proteome level and provides a high-resolution resource to link structural, functional, and metabolic diversity in the hippocampus. Further application of our high-resolution spatial proteomics will lay the foundation for studying HP development, circuit function, and disease-associated proteomic alterations.

articles.title: SDD: Synergistic Dual-Memory Debiasing for Semi-Supervised Continual Learning
articles.authors: Qiang Wang, Zeyu Peng, Bin Lu
articles.abstract: Semi-Supervised Continual Learning (SSCL) aims to enable deep learning models to learn incrementally from label-scarce streaming data without catastrophic forgetting. Existing SSCL methods face two core issues: severe overfitting to limited labeled samples, and accumulated feature representation bias across incremental tasks. To address these issues, we propose Synergistic Dual-Memory Debiasing (SDD), a semi-supervised continual learning framework that integrates Dual Memory Replay with unbiased contrastive debiasing. It includes two tightly coupled core components: a Dual Memory Replay (DMR) strategy with confidence-aware sampling, which avoids aggravating overfitting to limited labeled samples and an Unbiased Contrastive Learning (UCL) module with balanced KL regularization, which mitigates accumulated feature bias. Extensive experiments on three standard benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100) show that SDD achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art SSCL methods, with a maximum 4.98% accuracy gain over the NNCSL baseline.

articles.title: Quantitative Analysis of Electroencephalography in Hypnosis: A Neurophysiological Approach.
articles.authors: Baghdadi G, Motie Nasrabadi A.
articles.venue: The International journal of clinical and experimental hypnosis
articles.abstract: Hypnosis is a unique state of consciousness marked by heightened response to suggestions, focused attention, and altered cognitive control. This article explores the neural connections involved in hypnosis through electroencephalography (EEG) studies, examining brain changes during hypnosis and their relationship to hypnotic depth and susceptibility. Theta waves, linked to hypnotic depth, are stronger in highly hypnotizable individuals, while gamma waves are associated with focus, suggestion acceptance, and emotional responses. Hypnosis also induces frequency-dependent reorganization of large-scale brain connectivity, particularly in frontal-parietal and attentional networks, enhancing subjective experiences and responsiveness. EEG patterns reveal more dynamic neural activity during hypnosis, which cannot be captured by linear metrics alone. Hemispheric analysis shows greater left-hemisphere activity in highly hypnotizable individuals, particularly in emotionally and verbally mediated tasks, challenging the right-hemisphere dominance model. Event related potential (ERP) findings show that hypnosis affects information processing at both pre-attentional and cognitive levels. These insights contribute to understanding hypnosis' impact on the brain and its potential for personalized therapeutic interventions.

articles.title: LaLa-World: Scaling Latent World Models with Natural Language Actions
articles.authors: Junha Song, Geonmo Gu, Jeongeun Park
articles.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.

articles.title: Brain-inspired predictive visual attention for spatiotemporal semantic understanding of complex film and television videos
articles.authors: Peng Han
articles.abstract: Due to the unique characteristics of film and television, such as montage editing and narrative structure jumps, semantically salient targets frequently experience temporal feature drift, making it difficult for existing models to maintain stable semantic understanding output when keyframes are lost. Inspired by predictive coding mechanisms in neuroscience, this paper proposes a spatiotemporal joint representation framework driven by brain-like visual attention. A pixel-level saliency heatmap is constructed using eye-tracking data as a physiological-level supervisory signal. A Dual-Stream Spatio-Temporal Encoding Network (DS-STEN) is designed: the spatial stream uses ResNet to extract single-frame salient features, while the temporal stream uses 3D convolution to model the optical flow field and capture cross-frame trajectories. A Kalman filter-driven predictive attention module is introduced into the fusion layer to estimate the target’s position and feature distribution in the next frame. The prediction results are injected into the temporal stream as a priori mask to actively correct abnormal responses during drift. The corrected spatiotemporal features are aggregated with semantic context through a Transformer cross-frame self-attention layer and input into a semantic classification head to generate scene-level and event-level labels. End-to-end joint training is performed using a weighted loss of saliency prediction, trajectory consistency, and semantic classification. Experiments show that the saliency prediction correlation coefficient (CC) reaches 0.846 and the normalized scanpath saliency (NSS) reaches 2.47 on the AIM2024 benchmark. In the TVQA+ dataset target tracking task, the cross-frame tracking accuracy in unoccluded scenes reaches 95.3%. In the MovieNet dataset scene semantic classification task, the average accuracy for Dialogue scenes reaches 93.5%. This paper provides a new spatiotemporal modeling paradigm with a neuroscience basis for semantic understanding of complex film and television videos.

articles.title: Loneliness relates to smaller hippocampal subfield volumes in individuals with elevated plasma pTau217: results from IGNITE.
articles.authors: Martín-Fuentes I, Inagaki TK, Solis-Urra P, Oberlin LE, Sewell KR, Karikari TK, Zeng X, Kang C, Morris JK, Ripperger HS, Grove GA, Huang H, Sutton BP, Wan L, Vidoni ED, Marsland AL, Hillman CH, McAuley E, Kramer AF, Burns JM, Erickson KI.
articles.abstract: Loneliness is associated with cognitive decline and dementia risk, but the role of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology in its associations with medial temporal lobe (MTL) morphology remains unclear. We examined whether loneliness was related to total hippocampal volume, hippocampal subfields, and entorhinal cortex (ERC) volumes, and whether plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217) moderated these relationships. We analyzed baseline data from cognitively unimpaired older adults aged 65-80 years enrolled in IGNITE. Loneliness was assessed using the revised UCLA Loneliness Scale. Structural 3 T MRI included a high-resolution T2-weighted hippocampal sequence. Hippocampal subfields and ERC volumes were extracted using ASHS, and FreeSurfer estimated total hippocampal volume and intracranial volume. Participants were classified as pTau217-positive or negative using an Aβ-PET-calibrated threshold (> 0.46 pg/mL). Covariate-adjusted linear regression models tested loneliness associations and loneliness×pTau217 interactions. We included 601 participants (69.8 ± 3.7 years; 72.2% female; 76.4% White); 582 had usable pTau217 data, of whom 28.9% were pTau217-positive. pTau217 moderated associations with CA3 (β = - 0.215, 95% CI - 0.381 to - 0.048) and ERC (β = - 0.167, 95% CI - 0.318 to - 0.016), with negative associations observed among pTau217-positive but not pTau217-negative participants. Greater loneliness was associated with smaller total hippocampal volume (β = - 0.077, 95% CI, - 0.147 to - 0.007, p = 0.031), but not with individual subfields. Loneliness showed biomarker-dependent associations with MTL subfields, suggesting that pTau217-defined biological risk may modify links between psychosocial factors and neuroanatomical vulnerability. This biomarker-informed framework may help explain heterogeneity in prior loneliness-neuroimaging findings.Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02875301.
